clue.text: A vital matter comes first

definitions.text: A vital matter comes first

parts.note: the living substance of a cell is the matter of life, and its name opens with the Greek prefix for 'first'

explanation.surface: Something of life-or-death importance takes priority over everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital' reads as 'urgent', but here it means 'of life': the clue describes the living stuff of cells, whose name begins with proto-, Greek for first.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the jelly-like living material inside cells, literally 'first-formed substance' in Greek.

clue.text: Money to blue or otherwise

definitions.text: Money

indicators.note: 'otherwise' asks for the letters of the two words to be set out in a different order

explanation.surface: Cash used to make someone feel blue, or the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' rearranges BLUE + OR into the Russian currency; 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: The rouble is the unit of currency of Russia.

clue.text: Holiday tradesmen ?

definitions.text: Holiday tradesmen ?

parts.note: the 'trade' here is the tour: people whose holiday business is going round the sights

explanation.surface: A question about shopkeepers who are on their holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tradesmen' suggests shopkeepers; the question mark warns that the clue means people whose business on holiday is touring.
explanation.definitionFit: Holidaymakers travelling for pleasure are sightseers on a tour.

clue.text: Pets arrive, oddly enough, for Marques

definitions.text: Marques

indicators.note: 'oddly enough' tells the solver the letters of these two words arrive in an odd, mixed-up order

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, family pets turn up for a special breed of car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marques' looks like car brands; here it is the old 'letters of marque', licences that let private ships raid enemy shipping. 'oddly enough' rearranges PETS ARRIVE; 'for' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships sailing under a letter of marque were privately owned raiders licensed by a government, so the licence holders stand for the ships.

clue.text: About ten a girl put out a feeler

definitions.text: a feeler

indicators.note: 'About' puts the girl's name round the number, as if encircling it

parts.note: Anna is a girl's name
the number ten written out in letters

explanation.surface: A girl of about ten sends out a tentative enquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a girl aged about ten; in the wordplay 'About' means 'around', the girl's name encircling the number. 'put out' and 'a' only join the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: An insect's antenna is the sensory organ it uses for touch, a feeler.

clue.text: What a way to serve Murphy!

definitions.text: What a way to serve Murphy!

parts.words: What a way to serve Murphy!
parts.note: 'Murphy' is old slang for a potato (from the common Irish surname), and the clue asks how one is served

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the way someone named Murphy has been treated.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy looks like a man badly treated; it is slang for a potato, and one way to serve potatoes is pounded soft.
explanation.definitionFit: Potatoes boiled and pounded smooth make a common British side dish.

clue.text: It's beastly to run away with a worker

definitions.text: It's beastly

parts.note: the worker ant is the crossword's usual worker
to elope is to run away to marry

explanation.surface: It is a dreadful thing to run off with one of the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beastly' reads as 'awful'; it really means 'a beast', an animal. 'with' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a swift, horned grazing animal, so it is literally a beast.

clue.text: It doesn't serve to show all that's in store for us

definitions.text: It doesn't serve to show all that's in store for us

parts.words: It doesn't serve to show all that's in store for us
parts.note: 'in store' means inside a big shop, where each section shows only part of the stock on sale

explanation.surface: A gloomy line about not being told the whole of what the future holds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's in store for us' sounds like fate; read literally it is the goods in a large shop, each section of which displays only part of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A large shop is divided into sections, each selling one kind of goods.

clue.text: Una and Eve join forces, in a way

definitions.text: a way

indicators.note: the two women's names are pooled together and their letters regrouped

explanation.surface: Two women team up, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'join forces' pools UNA and EVE and rearranges them; 'in' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad tree-lined road or street is one kind of way.

clue.text: Arty type unappreciative of our present ?

definitions.text: Arty type unappreciative of our present ?

parts.words: Arty type unappreciative of our present ?
parts.note: 'present' means the present time, not a gift: an artist who looks only to what is to come

explanation.surface: An artistic person who is ungrateful for a gift we gave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' suggests a gift; it means the present day, which this artist despises in favour of times to come. The name was also used for an early 20th-century art movement.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist of the modern movement that rejected the past and celebrated speed and machines of the coming age.

clue.text: They don't live from day to day

definitions.text: They don't live from day to day

parts.words: They don't live from day to day
parts.note: 'live from day to day' usually means scraping by; read literally, these things last no longer than a single day

explanation.surface: People who do not live hand to mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom suggests people who are not poor; literally it describes things that do not survive from one day into the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayflies and other short-lived things last only a day, from the Greek for 'lasting a day'.

clue.text: Cuts the colours, we hear

definitions.text: Cuts

indicators.note: 'we hear' means the word is to be taken by its sound

parts.note: hues are colours or shades; the answer also runs backwards across 'colours, we hear', but that is a coincidence, not the setter's device

explanation.surface: Someone tones down the colours, it is reported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' says that HUES (colours) sounds like the answer, which means chops.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop with an axe or blade, so the verb here is the third-person form of chopping.

clue.text: One of those " many happy returns ", perhaps ?

definitions.text: One of those " many happy returns ", perhaps ?

parts.words: One of those " many happy returns ", perhaps ?
parts.note: 'many happy returns' is a birthday greeting, read literally as a joyful return to one's house

explanation.surface: A question about one of those birthday greetings.
explanation.walkthrough: The birthday greeting is taken literally: each happy return to one's house is an instance.
explanation.definitionFit: The joyful arrival back at one's house after a long absence.

clue.text: A newcomer who needs to watch his step ?

definitions.text: A newcomer who needs to watch his step ?

parts.words: A newcomer who needs to watch his step ?
parts.note: 'watch his step' means be careful, and literally a novice with a sore foot must tread carefully

explanation.surface: A new arrival who must be careful not to put a foot wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The novice's name splits as tender (sore) + foot, which is why he must watch where he treads.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice or inexperienced beginner, especially a new arrival in rough country.

clue.text: I represent unusual initiative

definitions.text: initiative

indicators.note: 'unusual' says the letters of the two words are to be set in a new, unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone claims to stand for unusual resourcefulness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges I REPRESENT; the boast reads like a candidate's slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: Enterprise is readiness to take on bold new projects, which is to say initiative.

clue.text: A lion goes to this church in Herefordshire

definitions.text: A lion goes to this church in Herefordshire

parts.words: A lion goes to this church in Herefordshire
parts.note: Leo, the lion, placed before the church word gives ..., a town in Herefordshire

explanation.surface: A lion wanders into a church somewhere in the English county of Herefordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: LEO (the lion of the zodiac) put before the answer, a large church, gives Leominster, a market town in Herefordshire, an English county bordering Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A minster is a large or important church, originally one attached to a monastery.

clue.text: Like Mr X describing a Wilkie Collins novel ?

definitions.text: Like Mr X describing a Wilkie Collins novel ?

parts.words: Like Mr X describing a Wilkie Collins novel ?
parts.note: Mr X is an anonymous person, and Wilkie Collins wrote a novel called No Name

explanation.surface: Someone compares an unnamed man to a character in a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins (1824-89) wrote the novel No Name; the adjective fits both an anonymous Mr X and that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Being without a name, as an anonymous person is.

clue.text: A well-knit jumper, for example ?

definitions.text: A well-knit jumper, for example ?

parts.note: 'jumper' is British for a sweater, but here is a high jumper, and 'well-knit' means of strong build

explanation.surface: A nicely knitted sweater, offered as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater, which suits 'well-knit'; here it is someone who jumps, with a well-knit (sturdy) frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A sportsperson such as a high jumper is a trained competitor in track and field.

clue.text: It can be said to high-light our way of life

definitions.text: It can be said to high-light our way of life

parts.words: It can be said to high-light our way of life
parts.note: 'high-light' is split literally: it lights our way from a height

explanation.surface: Something that showcases the way we live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high-light' looks like 'emphasise'; taken literally it is a light held high over the road we walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall post carrying a street light beside a road.

clue.text: Not exclusively a High Church feature

definitions.text: Not exclusively a High Church feature

parts.words: Not exclusively a High Church feature
parts.note: 'High Church' is the ritualist wing of Anglicanism, but read literally it is any church's high part

explanation.surface: A remark that some practice is not confined to ritualist Anglicans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High Church' suggests the Anglo-Catholic tradition; the clue means the lofty part of a church building, found in all traditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tower topped by a spire, rising from a church.

clue.text: His type should be easily recognizable

definitions.text: His type should be easily recognizable

parts.words: His type should be easily recognizable
parts.note: 'type' means printing type rather than a kind of person

explanation.surface: Someone's sort of character ought to be easy to spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His type' sounds like his kind of person; it is the metal type a printer sets, which must be legible.
explanation.definitionFit: A printer who sets type by hand or machine for a page.

clue.text: A large number consume it

definitions.text: A large number consume it

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a large number
to consume food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Many people eat this.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition (food most people eat) and also the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Animal flesh as food is eaten by most people.

clue.text: " When men were all the snow came flying" (Bridges)

definitions.text: " When men were all the snow came flying" (Bridges)

parts.words: " When men were all the snow came flying" (Bridges)
parts.note: a quotation with a word missing, from Robert Bridges' poem London Snow

explanation.surface: A line of poetry about snow falling in the night.
explanation.walkthrough: The line opens Robert Bridges' London Snow; the page prints a dash for the missing word after 'all', and the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow fell while everyone slept, unconscious in the night.

clue.text: Once the current name for Lancashire workers ?

definitions.text: Once the current name for Lancashire workers ?

parts.words: Once the current name for Lancashire workers ?
parts.note: 'current' means a flow of water, and Lancashire was the home of cotton mills, whose workers could be called a race

explanation.surface: A question about what Lancashire's workforce used to be called.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancashire, in north-west England, was the centre of the cotton-mill industry. The mill workers could be called the mill race, and the term is also the stream ('current') that drove a waterwheel.
explanation.definitionFit: The channel of fast water that turns a mill's wheel.

clue.text: They are not affected only by composers

definitions.text: They are not affected only by composers

parts.words: They are not affected only by composers
parts.note: composers write tunes, but the word for tunes also means the affected manners people put on

explanation.surface: A remark about who is touched by something besides composers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' means 'put on': people put on graces and pretensions, and composers write melodies; one word covers both.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both melodies and pretentious manners put on to impress.

clue.text: Not necessarily the occupant of a penthouse

definitions.text: Not necessarily the occupant of a penthouse

parts.words: Not necessarily the occupant of a penthouse
parts.note: 'penthouse' is split as 'pent house', a house in which someone is penned up

explanation.surface: A remark that not every luxury top-floor flat holds a rich tenant.
explanation.walkthrough: A penthouse is a smart top-floor flat; read as 'pent house', it is a place where someone is shut in, such as a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone held in a jail is shut in, or pent up.

clue.text: Old king goes three points to the right

definitions.text: Old king

parts.note: N, E and S are three compass points: north, east and south
taken as written
R is the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An ancient monarch turns through three points of the compass to face right.
explanation.walkthrough: Nestor was the aged, wise king of Pylos in Homer's Iliad; 'goes' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend he was the elderly king of Pylos who advised the Greeks at Troy.

clue.text: You need a potter's eye to make this plate

definitions.text: You need a potter's eye to make this plate

parts.words: You need a potter's eye to make this plate
parts.note: 'plate' is a printing plate cast in metal, not a dish a potter shapes

explanation.surface: Making this dish requires the trained eye of a potter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potter' and 'plate' suggest crockery; the plate is a cast metal printing plate, and the word also means a fixed, conventional image.
explanation.definitionFit: A solid metal plate cast from a mould of set type, used for printing.
